entries.title: Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes
entries.summary: Local authorities said several civilians were killed and dozens more wounded across Ukraine by Russian strikes. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has rejected Volodymyr Zelenskyy's proposal to meet with the Russian leader in Miami.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes

September 12, 2026

Local authorities said several civilians were killed and dozens more wounded across Ukraine by Russian strikes. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has rejected Volodymyr Zelenskyy's proposal to meet with the Russian leader in Miami.

Russia continued on Saturday its constant strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, killing at least four people and wounding dozens more.

According to Ukrainian officials, two people were killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, while steelmaker ArcelorMittal reported that two more people were killed at its plant in Kryvyi Rih, a city in the center of the country.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said that a Russian strike on an apartment building in Odesa wounded 37 people and that rescue teams are searching for two missing individuals.

He added that ten regions came under Russian attack last night and that Russian attack drones are still flying over many of them.

Ukraine retaliates by hitting chemical plants

In response to Russian attacks, Kyiv is fighting back. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has attacked "chemical enterprises" in the Perm region of the Urals and in the Samara region, which is located southwestern Russia.

The General Staff in Kyiv also reported a fire at a rubber factory in Togliatti, located in the Samara region. According to their statement, the company specializes in producing synthetic rubber important for tactical and ballistic missiles.

Togliatti Mayor, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person was hospitalized following a massive attack on the city. He added that several multi-story residential buildings were damaged.

Kremlin rebuffs Zelenskyy's meeting proposal

In an exclusive interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit in Miami in December.

However, on Saturday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow has yet to decide whether Putin will travel to the summit. "We don't know yet ​whether we'll be going to ​Miami," Peskov said, according to Russian media.

Commenting on Zelenskiy's proposal, Peskov reiterated Moscow's longstanding position that if the Ukrainian leader wants to meet with the Russian leader, he should come to Moscow.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Bulgaria: Fire at factory making munitions for Ukraine
entries.summary: Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions factory for links to an explosion at a similar facility in August. Arms maker EMCO says no human error was involved, as investigators look at sabotage.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria: Fire at factory making munitions for Ukraine

September 12, 2026

Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions factory for links to an explosion at a similar facility in August. Arms maker EMCO says no human error was involved, as investigators look at sabotage.

Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO.

Police say the blaze broke out Friday night and follows a similar incident at another EMCO site in August.

EMCO's munitions are used in Ukraine and sabotage has not been ruled out, video images of the fire broadcast locally showed it illuminating the night sky near the village of Tsareva Livada.

The full extent of the damage is not yet known but no casualties have been reported.

"At present there is no danger to the population," said local police, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off.

EMCO has ruled out any possibility of human error in the incident.

Bulgarian authorities investigating

On Saturday, Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan ​Demerdzhiev announced an investigation, saying, "We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, in order ‌to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern."

EMCO production facilities manager Slavcho Dimiev confirmed the fire as well, saying the site mainly ⁠stores ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-caliber rounds.

Dimiev told reporters additional security measures should ⁠be considered to protect arms ​facilities.

"If it is ultimately concluded that they [arms facilities] have been targeted," he said, "this is not an attack on a particular company alone; it is an attack on the national interest."

EMCO fire latest of several attacks attributed to Russia

NATO member-state Bulgaria has supported Kyiv's self-defense efforts since Russian forces invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

And EMCO, like other European arms manufacturers, has been the target of repeated sabotage.

The company is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, the survivor of an assassination attempt that authorities there say was carried out by Russian operatives. Three Russian nationals were charged over the incident.

In 2024, ​Bulgaria also issued arrest warrants for six Russian nationals that prosecutors say were involved in the destruction of EMCO arms depots storing munitions set for export to Ukraine ⁠and Georgia ​between 2011 and 2020.

At the time, prosecutors argued that they had uncovered links between the attempt on Gebrev, sabotage at Bulgarian arms depots and explosions at a munitions depot in the Czech Republic in 2014.

Arms manufacturers previously targeted

Friday's fire at EMCO echoes a number of recent attacks targeting European arms makers supplying Ukraine.

On August 13, the KNDS Ammo Italy arms manufacturing facility outside Rome was rocked by an explosion. Although the Italian government said it had no reason to believe that Russia was behind the attack, the Franco-German defense company said the incident was under investigation.

On September 3, incendiary devices were thrown near the Munich headquarters of defense technology company Rohde & Schwarz.

EMCO's Gebrev is not alone in being targeted either.

In 2024, US and German intelligence uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the CEO of Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.

In all instances, Russia has denied involvement, calling accusations, European war mongering.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump's trip to Ireland to watch a golf tournament has also included meetings with leaders there.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'

September 12, 2026

US President Donald Trump's trip to Ireland to watch a golf tournament has also included meetings with leaders there.

US President Donald Trump has said he would "love" to see the Republic of Ireland, an EU member, unite with British-run ⁠Northern Ireland as he faced reporters' questions on a range of issues on Saturday.

Trump is taking the weekend trip largely to watch the Irish Open golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country’s Atlantic coast, but he met as well with the Irish president and prime minister, or taoiseach.

The US leader also spoke optimistically about his country's war with Iran and its trade conflict with Canada, among several other topics.

What did Trump say about Ireland?

After a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in the capital, Dublin, Trump said he very much supported what he said would be the eventual unification of the two parts of the island of Ireland.

"Well, I don't want to ​cause any problems, ​but ‌I will tell you, I'd love to see ‌it unified," Trump told ‌reporters.

"The way I look at it, it's ⁠going ​to happen ​eventually ... I think it would ​be a ‌fantastic thing," he added.

"Now the UK will have ​something ⁠to say about it ... but ⁠I think ​it would be a great thing."

The British government responded swiftly to the remarks, with Prime Minister Andy Burham's office saying that in his view, there was no majority public support for a referendum on the issue and that there would not be another one until that changed.

Previous US presidents have avoided touching on the subject in view of the delicate nature of the issue, with Northern Ireland seeing decades of of deadly sectarian violence in the 20th century over the question of whom it should belong to.

What did Trump say about the Iran war?

Trump also said that the US war with Iran, which began on February 28, would "end very soon" — a view he has frequently expressed in the past, but which has not yet materialized.

He also said that the end of the conflict would mean that the price of oil, which has soared as a result of the war, would "come tumbling down."

However, he vehemently defended his decision to mount the military operation against Iran.

He said that the US attacked because "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon", adding: "They were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."

"If they had it, they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East, and they would have hit some [...] in my opinion, [of] Europe's cities and beyond cities, and they would probably hit us soon before we put out the fire. But they cannot have a nuclear weapon."

The war with Iran is not supported by a majority of the US population, particularly in view of promises made by Trump on the campaign trail to keep his country out of foreign "forever" conflicts.

What did Trump say about Canada?

The president sounded a similarly optimistic note regarding the US trade war with Canada.

He said Canada was keen to make a deal and that one could be struck "fairly soon," while reiterating his claims that Canada had treated US farmers unfairly with its tariffs.

"Canada ‌wants to make a ‌deal ​very badly," he said.

"Canada has ​to treat our farmers better. ​They can't ‌charge our farmers tariffs," he said, ​adding: "You'll ⁠probably see a deal with Canada ⁠fairly ​soon."

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
entries.summary: A funeral is underway for King Oyo Nyimba, who was crowned in the Tooro Kingdom in 1995 aged just 3. His death at 34 has triggered a dispute over a successor, as rumors abound of possible heirs born out of wedlock.
entries.content:
Uganda

Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row

September 12, 2026

A funeral is underway for King Oyo Nyimba, who was crowned in the Tooro Kingdom in 1995 aged just 3. His death at 34 has triggered a dispute over a successor, as rumors abound of possible heirs born out of wedlock.

Uganda has concluded a nine-day period of mourning for King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, with a funeral for the Tooro Kingdom's late monarch due to take place in the western city of Fort Portal on Saturday.

Oyo, who once held the unofficial title of the world's youngest king, ascended the throne as a young child in 1995 and died last month of cancer aged just 34, with his death prompting a bitter succession dispute.

How is Oyo to be laid to rest?

The casket carrying the king's body, which was draped in the blue-and-yellow Tooro flag, was carried by hearse from the royal palace in Fort Portal in a procession accompanied by royal guards dressed in orange tunics and beating wooden sticks.

The ceremony in St. John's Cathedral was to be attended by hundreds of mourners, including senior Ugandan government officials.

After the service in the cathedral, Oyo was to be buried at the site of the royal tombs.

At the burial ceremony, tradition dictates that the successor should throw nine coffee berries into the grave.

Dispute over Oyo's successor

However, the question of that successor has aroused considerable controversy, and it was in doubt until late on Friday who would carry out that rite.

On Wednesday, a committee made up of members of the royal clan announced it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, as the new king.

Kijanangoma, 54, is a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC.

But the immediate family of the late king said that the latter's will had called for a son who was born out of wedlock and has yet to be identified to succeed him.

Additionally, there have been claims on social media that there are at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo's children.

Those supporting Kijanangoma say Oyo's family has so far failed to come up with concrete information on the alleged son, while traditionalists also favor the choice of an adult as new monarch.

A source with knowledge ⁠of ​crisis talks on the matter said authorities had managed to get Kijanangoma officially accepted as successor on Friday.

Beloved traditional monarchs

Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined the family's ability to mourn the king's death.

"I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: Please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Although Uganda is led by an elected head of state, it still possesses several kingdoms that were restored in 1993 after being banned for some three decades following the country's independence from British colonial rule.

The monarchs of such kingdoms are often beloved but hold no formal power. Instead they are seen as guardians of traditional identity and heritage.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: BRICS summit leaders urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East
entries.summary: The joint declaration at the BRICS 2026 summit expressed 'deep concern' over hostilities in the Middle East. China's President Xi Jinping said the Iran war was not in the bloc's interest. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Asia

BRICS declaration urges 'maximum restraint' in Middle East

Published September 11, 2026last updated September 12, 2026

The joint declaration at the BRICS 2026 summit expressed 'deep concern' over hostilities in the Middle East. China's President Xi Jinping said the Iran war was not in the bloc's interest. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian PM Modi has announced the adoption of a joint declaration
  • The BRICS coalition expressed concern over escalations in the Middle East
  • Modi will meet China's Xi on the sidelines of BRICS today
  • Putin and Modi discuss a wide range of issues, including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors
  • Modi again urges Putin to end the war in Ukraine
  • Modi calls for maritime trade to be protected during bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New Delhi
  • Pezeshkian warns Iran coming under 'critical, dangerous' US economic pressure

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India, China to work towards resolving disputed border — New Delhi

India, China to work towards resolving disputed border — New Delhi

India and China have "expressed commitment" to normalizing their disputed border, India's Foreign Ministry said.

"The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question," the ministry said as Chinese President Xi Jinping visits New Delhi for a BRICS summit.

The ministry added the Prime Minister Narendra Modi "underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues."

"Differences should not become disputes," it said.

The statement said that Modi stressed that China and India both "must be guided by three mutuals — mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest."

Both India and China maintain heavy military deployments along their 3,500 kilometer (2,175-mile) border along Kashmir and Tibet.

Chinese and Indian troops engaged in several skirmishes along the disputed border in 2020 and 2021.

Skip next section China 'willing to work with fellow BRICS members' towards achieving Middle East peace, says Xi

China 'willing to work with fellow BRICS members' towards achieving Middle East peace, says Xi

Speaking at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for greater efforts to promote peace in the Middle East and the Gulf region.

"China is willing to work with fellow BRICS members to play due role in achieving peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region," President Xi Jinping told the official Xinhua news agency in New Delhi.

"The war has caused serious losses to people across the region and does not serve the common interests of the international community," Xi added, according to Xinhua.

Xi also pointed out that power politics are on the rise, the international order is being challenged and there are growing shortcomings in terms of peace and security. The BRICS nations must stand "on the right side of history," he urged.

Skip next section What does the joint declaration say?

What does the joint declaration say?

On the first day of the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of a joint declaration.

The joint declaration adopted by the BRICS coalition calls for "maximum restraint" in the Middle East.

"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the statement read.

The member states have reiterated their commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy.

The declaration also advocates for a multilateral approach that respects diverse national viewpoints and positions on crucial global issues.

The declaration comes at a time ​when the US and Iran have resumed tit-for-tat strikes ​against each ‌other, after a pause in fighting for much of August.

Since the bloc inlcuded Iran and US-ally UAE both, it was expected that reaching a concensus will be difficult.

Additionally, the bloc expressed concerns ‌about the rise of "unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures" that distort trade, against the backdrop ​of US sanctions ⁠against Tehran amid its war with the country, and against Russia ⁠over its ​conflict with Ukraine.

The bloc stressed on the need to cooperate to maintain the smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy.

Skip next section What does a joint declaration against war mean for the bloc's influence?

What does a joint declaration against war mean for the bloc's influence?

"It’s all done," Indian prime minister Narendra Modi said. And what he meant was this: BRICS has an approved joint declaration for 2026. The leaders agreed on the text of the Delhi Declaration on day one of the summit after their plenary session.

It is important to keep in mind that, for the first six months of the Iran war, the grouping of Global South nations failed to issue a joint statement. The US-Israel-led attack on Iran has put enormous strain on the bloc.

The war directly involves three BRICS members: Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. But not as allies. Iran has attacked the UAE and Saudi Arabia, seeing them as proxies for the US.

The war has been devastating for the Global South, which BRICS represents. Think oil and fertilizers — and food security.

The compromise now found in Delhi appears to be a joint declaration condemning unilateral wars, without naming any country. 

That is rather low-key — but perhaps better than nothing, especially for BRICS chair India, which can claim this as a diplomatic victory. As former UN diplomat and prominent Indian foreign policy voice Shashi Tharoor had told me before the summit:

"There is very little doubt that all the BRICS members have not necessarily upheld the UN Charter, the inviolability of borders, the sovereignty of member states of the UN, and the inadmissibility of the use of force to settle international disputes."

The BRICS countries now number 11 and represent about half of the world’s population. And when economies are measured by what people can actually buy, they account for around 40 percent of global economic output.

So BRICS leaders feel they have a strong case for criticizing western political hegemony and the dominance of the US dollar. They argue that global institutions such as the UN, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank no longer reflect the rising power of emerging economies and the Global South.

In his opening address, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that reform of the UN Security Council cannot wait any longer.

Skip next section Xi says US-Iran war doesn't serve "common interests": Xinhua

Xi says US-Iran war doesn't serve "common interests": Xinhua

Speaking during the BRICS Summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping said that the Middle East war, sparked by US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, does not serve the world's interests, Beijing's state media reported.

"As the situation in the Middle East and the Gulf region continues to evolve, the war there has caused serious losses to people across the region," state news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying in New Delhi, which is hosting the 18th BRICS summit attended by leaders including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

It "does not serve the common interests of the international community", Xi said, according to Xinhua.

Skip next section BRICS reaches consensus, Modi announces joint declaration

BRICS reaches consensus, Modi announces joint declaration

In his closing remarks for the first session at the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the BRICS ‌group ⁠of nations ⁠unanimously ​adopted a ​joint declaration ​on ‌Saturday, the first day ‌of their ‌annual ​summit in New Delhi.

Reuters news agency, citing four anonymous sources, had earlier in the day reported that members of the BRICS coalition have agreed on a joint declaration which does not name any country but will condemn unilateral ​war by any country.

The members include Brazil, ​Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, ​Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

Skip next section Can BRICS Really Challenge the Dollar? Not Quite, Says BRICS Expert

Can BRICS Really Challenge the Dollar? Not Quite, Says BRICS Expert

As leaders gather in New Delhi for the 2026 BRICS Summit, talk of "de-dollarization" is everywhere. But Anuradha Mitra Chenoy, Professor and former dean at School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, argues the real story is more modest, and more interesting.

Every BRICS summit now comes with the same headline: is this the moment the bloc finally dethrones the US dollar? For Chenoy, the question itself is the problem.

"The debate is often overstated," she told DW. BRICS countries, in her reading, are not on a mission to replace the dollar. What they are doing is settling more of their bilateral trade in local currencies — a shift that has less to do with ideology than with practicality. It cuts transaction costs, speeds up payments, and makes trade more predictable for businesses that used to route everything through dollars by default.

A dollar that’s been "weaponized"

If there’s a political edge to this trend, Chenoy locates it elsewhere, in how the dollar itself has been used as a tool of coercion. US sanctions, tariffs, and the freezing or outright confiscation of foreign reserves have all pushed countries, particularly across the Global South, to think harder about their exposure to the American financial system.

That calculus matters most for heavily indebted developing economies. By trading directly in local currencies with partners like India, China, Russia, and South Africa, these countries can sidestep some of their need to hold dollars just to settle trade. The payoff, Chenoy says, is twofold. Firstly, lower transaction costs, and secondly, in some cases, less reliance on dollar-denominated debt.

India’s balancing act

New Delhi has backed greater use of local currencies and cross-border payment mechanisms within BRICS, even as it keeps its economic relationship with Washington firmly intact.

For Chenoy, It’s also not a new one. She points back to the Rupee-Ruble trading arrangement India ran with the Soviet Union decades ago — a reminder that local-currency trade has deep roots in Indian economic policy, long before "de-dollarization" became a buzzword.

Chenoy says what’s actually happening inside BRICS — not a coordinated campaign to topple the dollar, but a pragmatic hedge that countries are spreading their financial risk across more currencies and more systems, one bilateral deal at a time.

Skip next section Modi meets Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince on sidelines of BRICS Summit

Modi meets Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince on sidelines of BRICS Summit

Modi met with Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi.

The two leaders met at Hyderabad House in New Delhi, where they sought to further strengthen their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

The United Arab Emirates became a full member of BRICS in January 2024, along with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Modi and Sheikh Khaled welcomed the announcement by UAE-based International Holding Company (IHC) to invest in the development of an $11.5 billion (€9.91 billion integrated greenfield aluminium project in Odisha.

The project is expected to be India's largest integrated aluminium investment and position Odisha as a global hub for aluminium manufacturing.

The bilateral meeting between Modi and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince comes amid growing India-UAE cooperation, particularly in the areas of trade and energy security.

In a post on X, India's Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in the meeting, "the leaders reaffirmed commitment to deepening of the India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership."

Skip next section Modi holds bilateral meetings with PM of Ethiopia, Malaysia

Modi holds bilateral meetings with PM of Ethiopia, Malaysia

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held bilateral meetings with the Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed Ali and Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim on the sidelines of the ongoing BRICS Summit.

Modi thanked both the country heads for their participation in the event and reaffirmed strengthening the bilateral Strategic Partnership with both Malaysia and Ethiopia.

Modi's meeting with Abiy Ahmed Ali built further on his historic maiden bilateral visit to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia last year. The two leaders discussed improving cooperation in defence and economic sectors.

In the bilateral meeting with Ibrahim, both the leaders reviewed the results of Modi's visit to Malaysia earlier this year. A significant outcome of Modi's trip was Malaysia's agreement to the establishment of Consulate General of India in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah — a move that will increase India’s diplomatic and consular outreach in the region.

Following his meeting with Modi, Ibrahim in a post on X said, "we agreed to continue the momentum of the close Malaysia-India relationship and to strengthen the friendship rooted in a long history and warm ties between the peoples of both nations.

Skip next section India faces balancing act between US and China: DW's Head of Geopolitics reports from Delhi

India faces balancing act between US and China: DW's Head of Geopolitics reports from Delhi

The BRICS summit is packed with bilaterals for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Yesterday, he walked hand in hand with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hugged Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Today, he has already met the prime ministers of Ethiopia, Malaysia and Vietnam, as well as the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. More meetings are to follow as the clock counts down to 5:45 pm local time. That is when Modi is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping. And that's a big thing — especially for Indian media, which are broadcasting live around the clock.

Modi and Xi have, of course, met several times in recent years on the sidelines of multilateral summits — at the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024, and at the SCO summits in Tianjin in 2025 and Bishkek just two weeks ago. But Xi has not been to India since 2019. This will be his first visit to the country in seven years.

Relations between the two Asian powers froze after a deadly clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border, known as the Line of Actual Control. Direct flights and visas were suspended, while political engagement and trade ties suffered a major setback.

Today’s meeting could mark another step in the cautious thaw between the two nuclear-armed Asian powers, which have spent years drifting apart. But beneath the expected smiles and handshakes, deep mistrust remains — especially over their disputed border and over who gets to shape the future of Asia.

India's huge trade deficit with China might surface in discussions. Bilateral trade has nearly doubled in five years, but so has India's dependence on Chinese imports. Trade between the two countries reached $151.1 billion (€130.22 billion) in the 2025–26 financial year, making China India's largest trading partner. But the imbalance is striking: India imported $131.6 billion worth of goods from China, while exporting just $20 billion.

And when it comes to BRICS,India has no appetite for turning the bloc into an anti-Western platform that could jeopardize its relationship with the United States. A trade agreement with Washington is still pending, and India remains dependent on US technology. At the same time, China has become the world’s second-largest economy.

The elephant in the room here at BRICS 2026 in New Delhi, of course, is the US president. While Trump continues to threaten India with sanctions and tariffs for doing business with Iran and Russia, he is taking a softer line with China as he tries to get closer to Xi.

For New Delhi, then, the challenge is to deepen ties with China without drifting too far from the US — and to use BRICS to strengthen India's room for manoeuvre without turning it into an anti-Western alliance.

Skip next section Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Delhi

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Delhi

China's President Xi Jinping landed in Delhi this morning to attend the 18th BRICS Summit and hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"At noon on September 12, local time, President Xi Jinping arrived in New Delhi by special plane. He will attend the 18th BRICS summit at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi," Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said.

This is Xi's first visit to India since 2019, marking the biggest step toward normalizing ties between the two Asian powers, which took a major hit when India and China locked horns in the deadliest clash in over four decades over the disputed border in Ladakh's Galwan Valley.

The two countries have also sparred over Arunachal Pradesh's geographical names.

Xi's visit now signals the importance accorded by China to BRICS as well as maintaining ties with India.

Ahead of Xi's visit, in a post on X, China's ambassador to India Xu Feihong said that China will work with India to "properly handle differences" and "be friends enjoying good-neighborliness and partners helping each other succeed."

Modi and Xi are scheduled to meet on the sidelines of BRICS at 5.45 p.m. local time (1215 GMT). In their meeting, the two leaders are expected to focus on bilateral trade and border issues.

Skip next section Welcome back!

Welcome back!

We are resuming our coverage of the BRICS Summit 2026, taking place in New Delhi at the Bharat Mandapam.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held bilateral meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and UN Chief Antonio Guterres on the eve of the BRICS Summit.

Modi and Putin reaffirmed their ties. Both the leaders discussed key regional and global issues including the conflicts in the Middle East and the Ukraine war which was referred to as "conflicts in the Black Sea region."

In his meeting with Pezeshkian, Modi thanked the Iranian leader for his participation in the summit "despite the challenging circumstances" for Iran, which is at war with the US and Israel.

Modi also reiterated that "all issues must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy."

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

It's past midnight in New Delhi, so we are pausing our coverage for tonight.

We will be back on Saturday for the start of the two-day BRICS leaders' summit.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit

IN DEPTH: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit

New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Narendra Modi's diplomatic gains.

Find out more about India's diplomatic balancing act between BRICS members China and Russia and the West in this report by DW's Mural Krishnan.

Skip next section Modi urges Putin to end Ukraine war

Modi urges Putin to end Ukraine war

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi again appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.

During their meeting in New Delhi on the eve of the BRICS summit, Modi told Putin that dialogue and diplomacy are the right way to resolve conflicts, the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Russia's war in Ukraine and its impact on shipping in the Black Sea have affected India, a major buyer of Russian oil and grain. Indian sailors have also been caught up in drone attacks.

The war, which the Indian Foreign Ministry has referred to as conflicts "in the Black Sea region," is on the agenda for the two-day summit.

India has adopted a typically pragmatic approach to the conflict, seeking to balance ties with the West and with Russia.

However, during an August meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Kyrgyzstan, Modi urged Putin to end the war, which was in its fifth year.

entries.title: Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
entries.summary: A German newspaper has cited reports tying a failed attack at Leipzig Airport to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency. One suspect's ties to GRU were known when he entered the country, yet he was not surveilled.
entries.content:
Germany

Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports

September 12, 2026

A German newspaper has cited reports tying a failed attack at Leipzig Airport to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency. One suspect's ties to GRU were known when he entered the country, yet he was not surveilled.

Germany's Welt am Sonntag (WaS) newspaper has cited intelligence reports tying the recent failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport directly to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.

In an article published on Saturday, Welt am Sonntag said that a man with known ties to the GRU was responsible for operational logistics in the attempted attack.

Further, it said those ties were known to German authorities when the man entered the country from Turkey, nevertheless, he was not surveilled after arrival.

Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the Russian national is now in his home country after departing to Serbia on a flight from Berlin-Brandenburg Airport.

A second man, a Belarus citizen, was also cited as an accomplice in the report.

Explosives thought to have entered Germany from Bulgaria and Serbia

German intelligence sources said that the explosives used in the incident were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia and then stored in underground depots once they arrived in Leipzig.

Berlin quickly made clear that forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms used in other Russian hybrid attacks — pointed to a Russian plot.

In early August, German tabloid BILD reported that authorities had found DNA traces on the drone's remote control antenna. Those samples were said to have matched DNA found at the scene of a July 20, 2024, arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility operated by German courier company DHL.

Leipzig attack averted but Russian escalation will continue

The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine — occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was found near a Ukrainian transport jet.

Authorities were able to disarm the drone and after public speculation that Moscow was behind the incident the German government officially blamed Russia in early September.

Saturday's article said Berlin made the attribution on the basis of the intelligence reports cited.

In response to its conclusion, Germany announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.

The Kremlin in turn reacted by closing Goethe Institutes — a German cultural exchange outfit — across Russia.

As in numerous similar hybrid attacks prior, Russia has denied any involvement in the incident.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Brazil: Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before election
entries.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
entries.content:
Brazil

Flavio Bolsonaro faces graft probe weeks before Brazil vote

September 12, 2026

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to newly unsealed court documents.

What do we know about Bolsonaro's corruption probe?

The probe centers on funds Bolsonaro allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker behind the collapsed Banco Master, to help produce "Dark Horse," an unreleased film starring Jim Caviezel as the elder Bolsonaro.

Investigators are examining roughly $12 million that flowed from a Vorcaro-linked entity to a fund tied to Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother and campaign adviser, who lives in Texas. One document alleges Eduardo advised on how the money should be managed once in the United States.

Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation in July at the request of federal police, but the case remained sealed until Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered it made public this week, Reuters reported.

Federal police raided the production company behind the film and the office of congressman Mario Frias, its executive producer, on Thursday. Both have been barred from leaving the country and deny wrongdoing.

How did the Bolsonaros respond?

Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any misconduct, telling reporters at a campaign stop, "It is very positive that the documents are unsealed," the Associated Press reported

"I want transparency in everything."

Eduardo Bolsonaro similarly rejected the allegations, telling Reuters the funds were routed through the US to avoid interference from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw his father's coup conviction.

"They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn't," he said.

On social media, he said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.”

What did Lula say?

In a Thursday television interview, Lula said Banco Master "was created in the Bolsonaro administration" and shuttered during his own term. He has called for full transparency in the case regardless of political fallout.

The disclosures come three weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, in which polls show Bolsonaro and Lula roughly tied.

Political analysts say the timing leaves Bolsonaro less room to recover than when the scandal first surfaced in May, though the fallout could also cut against Lula given the case's ties to Vorcaro's dealings with multiple political and judicial figures.

A runoff, if needed, is set for October 25.

entries.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Ninos intensifying?
entries.summary: Records from the past few decades show that, during this period, El Nino events have been frequent and often extreme. But is this normal, or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a clear indication.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Corals as climate archive: Are El Ninos intensifying?

September 12, 2026

Records from the past few decades show that, during this period, El Nino events have been frequent and often extreme. But is this normal, or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a clear indication.

A storm is gathering. Most likely a very big one. El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon occurring every two to seven years, towards the end of the year, but it comes in various different strengths, depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Ninos are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases of greater than three degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.

The German Meteorological Service believes this "could in all likelihood develop into one of the strongest El Nino events since records began."

But a recent article by the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology states that whether or not strong El Nino events will intensify as a result of climate change "remains the subject of ongoing research."

The data gap: What corals can tell us about El Nino

The problem is that the data on ocean surface temperatures is only truly reliable from the 1980s onward, with the start of satellite observation. And this data doesn't tell us how El Nino behaved before industrialization and the burning of fossil fuels.

US researchers say corals can help to close this knowledge gap. Julia Cole, a climate scientist and paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan, and her team recently published a study on this subject in the journal Science.

"We've known for a long time that the last 40 or 50 years has really strong El Nino events," says Cole. "It's been hard to say whether the recent strong El Nino that we've had is part of a natural cycle, or if it's something a little bit unusual related to being in a warmer than normal world." The coral analysis points firmly in one direction: Unusual. Not normal.

Corals: A repository of 1,000 years of climate history

Cole and her team examined fossilized and living corals around the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador in the eastern Pacific. Corals grow between one and two centimeters per year, and in doing so form a structure similar to growth rings on trees. "We made use of the fact that corals record ocean temperatures as they grow, in the chemical composition of their skeleton," Cole explains.

Corals are living creatures that construct external skeletons through calcification, adding a band of new growth each year with calcium carbonate precipitated from the surrounding water. In this way, over decades and centuries, corals have formed entire reef systems. Other chemical elements are also incorporated into the skeleton during the calcification process — strontium, for example. Sometimes more is deposited, sometimes less, depending on the temperature of the water.

"In colder temperatures, it [the skeleton] absorbs more strontium, in warmer temperatures less," says Cole. The ratio of strontium to calcium in the skeleton provides information about changes in temperature.

Specific isotopes of oxygen in coral skeletons provide clues, as well. "The rare oxygen-18 and the common oxygen-16 are also taken up in a ratio that reflects temperature," says Cole. In colder conditions, more oxygen-18 is absorbed than in warmer temperatures.

In this way, researchers were able to reconstruct the changes in ocean temperatures over the past 1,000 years, according to the age of the corals. Their conclusion was that El Nino events have become markedly stronger compared to the pre-industrial period.

Corals give indications, not conclusive answers

Cole's study has confirmed a long-held suspicion. "These developments correspond to the predictions of the best climate models. They predict a quantifiably higher likelihood of extreme eastern Pacific El Nino events in the 2030s," says Jens Zinke, professor of paleobiology at the University of Leicester in England.

However, other scientists are more circumspect in assessing the study's significance. "Coral data does achieve a high temporal resolution — monthly to seasonal — but its accuracy is dependent on local conditions, meaning that direct comparisons with modern measurement data are fraught with uncertainty," says Andreas Fink, professor of meteorology at the Institute for Meteorology and Climate Research in Karlsruhe. According to Fink, the significance of the study is undermined by its regional limitation to the eastern Pacific.

Cole is also aware of her study's limitations. "Our data does fill a gap, but I want to be clear that our record isn't continuous," she says. "We don't have every single year over the last millennium. We have a little bit under half of the years covered."

Floods, droughts, record heat — the consequences of stronger El Ninos

Although the epicenter of the El Nino phenomenon is the Pacific, it changes the weather across the globe. In countries like Ecuador and Peru it can cause heavy rains and flooding, while Australia and Indonesia may experience a lack of rain, leading to drought and wildfires. El Niño also causes global temperatures to rise for a while.

If the predictions prove right and this El Nino does in fact become a Super El Nino, the coming year, 2027, will probably be another of record heatwaves, according to Thomas Felis. Felis leads the research group on coral paleoclimatology at the MARUM Center for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen, and has conducted a similar study to Cole's.

Heat-stressed oceans: El Nino is a threat for corals

A year of record heat "will very probably lead to another global coral bleaching," says Felis. This has happened before, in the years 2023–24 and 2015–16, which were also El Nino years.

Corals get their characteristic colors from certain algae with which they live in symbiosis. Through photosynthesis, the algae provide the energy the corals need to live. If the temperature of the ocean is too high, the algae start to produce toxins, and the corals end the partnership. The coral remains, in its skeleton.

It can survive like that for a few weeks, and if the temperature drops again, the algae return. "But if this state, with abnormally high summer temperatures, goes on for too long, the coral becomes so sick that it eventually dies," Felis explains.

Worldwide coral death would mean not just the end of a unique ecosystem, but the destruction of an archive that preserves the history of the oceans.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
entries.summary: Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance, and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.
entries.content:
Africa

Uber leaves two African markets — and drivers in despair

September 12, 2026

Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance, and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.

A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.

With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.

In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Africa a difficult market to crack

Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.

However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation: Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.

In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20% — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.

Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers

Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.

He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."

"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.

"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."

Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.

The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.

"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.

Their pleas and concerns, however, remain largely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.

Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, it comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.

This also makes consumers less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.

This is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."

The complex economics of ride-hailing

There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.

Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives."

"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber:

Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars.

Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?

As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles day after trilateral drills end
entries.summary: North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises Pyongyang had called provocative.
entries.content:
South Korea

North Korea fires missiles after US-South Korea drills

September 12, 2026

North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises Pyongyang had called provocative.

North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Saturday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped up a five-day trilateral military exercise that Pyongyang has criticized as provocative.

What do we know about the launches?

The missiles were fired from North Korea's eastern Wonsan area and traveled roughly 250 kilometers before landing in the country's eastern waters, South Korea's military said.

According to the Yonhap news agency, the North appears to have launched its Hwasong-11 series ballistic missiles alongside rounds from 600-millimeter multiple rocket launchers, with the two systems fired in succession across multiple instances, sources told the outlet.

The JCS said it had increased surveillance and was coordinating closely with the US and Japan. Meanwhile, South Korea's presidential national security council called on North Korea to halt launches that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions.

The US Pacific Command said the launches did not pose an immediate threat to American territory or regional allies, reaffirming Washington's defense commitments in the region.

What did the US-Korea drills entail?

The trilateral drills that preceded the launches, known as Freedom Edge, involved joint training across air, sea and cyber domains, including maritime maneuvers, air refueling and cyber coordination.

South Korea's military has described the exercises as defensive, intended to strengthen a coordinated response to North Korean nuclear threats.

North Korean Defense Minister Kim Song Gi had denounced the drills as "provocative" when they began earlier this week, threatening unspecified "strong and reflective countermeasures." 

Saturday's launch marked North Korea's first missile test in roughly three weeks, following a similar barrage of more than 10 short-range missiles last month during a separate round of US-South Korea exercises.

Has South Korea's relationship with the US changed?

The launches also come amid a broader shift in the security dynamic on the Korean Peninsula. 

Last month, President Donald Trump ordered a significant scaling back of the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea, citing his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who has long described the drills as rehearsals for invasion.

But Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the gesture, saying a shortened drill would not change its "provocative, aggressive nature." 

Last Sunday, Kim Jong Un used a ceremony marking the commissioning of North Korea's second naval destroyer to call for expanding the country's nuclear deterrent. Both of the country's destroyers are said to be capable of carrying nuclear-capable missiles.

The Associated Press experts say Pyongyang's leader, bolstered by his advancing weapons program and closer ties with Moscow and Beijing, may be positioning himself to extract greater concessions in potential talks with Washington. 

Kim has said he would consider returning to negotiations if the US drops what he calls its "hostile policy" and recognizes North Korea's status as a nuclear state.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez
